subject: Physics
title: Motion in a Straight Line
summary: This chapter builds the language of one-dimensional motion — position, displacement, velocity, acceleration and the three kinematic equations — and teaches you to read position-time and velocity-time graphs. There is no Class 11 board exam, but this chapter is tested in the school final and it is the base every kinematics question in Class 12, JEE and NEET is built on.

exam_profile.weightage: No CBSE board exam in Class 11. In the school final (and in most schools' unit tests), this chapter usually carries about 5–7 marks out of the mechanics unit, often as one graph-based question plus one numerical on the equations of motion.

question_types.note: Sign of velocity/acceleration from a graph, whether displacement can be zero while distance is not, or a quick numerical using v = u + at.
Tests whether you understand *why* a rule holds — e.g. why speed is never negative but velocity can be, or why acceleration can be nonzero at zero velocity (as at the top of a vertical throw).
Define a term, or read one value (velocity/acceleration) off a graph at a given instant.
A numerical using the three kinematic equations, or a relative-velocity problem with two bodies moving on the same line.
Derive the three kinematic equations by calculus or graphically, then apply one of them to a free-fall or braking-distance scenario.
A short passage (a car braking, a ball thrown up, two trains) followed by 4 sub-questions mixing concept and calculation.

hot_topics: Distance vs displacement, and when displacement is zero but distance is not
Average velocity vs average speed vs instantaneous velocity
Reading slope on a position–time graph and area under a velocity–time graph
Deriving v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², v² = u² + 2as (both calculus and graphical methods)
Motion under gravity: time to reach maximum height, maximum height, total time of flight
Relative velocity of two objects moving on the same straight line
Stopping distance and reaction time numericals
Interpreting whether a v–t or a–t graph is physically possible

sections.heading: 2.1 Introduction: Motion, Point Object and Frame of Reference
sections.body:
A body is said to be in motion if its position changes with time relative to a chosen reference point, called the origin, fixed in a frame of reference. Motion is always described relative to some observer — a passenger sitting still in a moving train is at rest with respect to the train but in motion with respect to the ground. There is no such thing as absolute motion.

When the size of a body is much smaller than the distance it travels, we treat it as a point object — its internal structure and rotation don't matter, only the position of one point. A train travelling several hundred kilometres can be treated as a point object for that journey, even though it cannot be treated as a point object while it is crossing a platform.

Motion in a straight line — also called rectilinear motion or one-dimensional motion — is the simplest case, where the object's position can be described by a single coordinate x measured along the line, with a sign showing direction. This chapter fixes the vocabulary (position, displacement, velocity, acceleration) that every later mechanics chapter reuses.
sections.tip: Whenever a question says 'with respect to the ground' or 'with respect to the train', it is testing frame of reference — answer relative to the frame named, not the one that feels natural.

sections.heading: 2.2 Position, Path Length and Displacement
sections.body:
Position is the location of the object with respect to the chosen origin, given a sign convention (usually right/up = positive). Path length (or distance) is the total length of the actual path travelled — it is a scalar and can only increase or stay the same. Displacement is the change in position, Δx = x2 − x1; it is a vector, so in one dimension it carries a sign showing direction, and it is the straight-line (shortest) separation between the initial and final position.

Displacement can be zero even when the path length is not: a body that returns exactly to its starting point has covered a nonzero distance but zero displacement. This is the single most repeated conceptual MCQ from this chapter. Displacement magnitude can never exceed the path length; the two are equal only when the motion is along a straight line without any reversal in direction.

Example: a man walks 8 m east then 6 m west. Path length = 8 + 6 = 14 m. Displacement = 8 − 6 = 2 m east (taking east as positive).
sections.tip: If a question gives a round trip (there and back to the same point), displacement = 0 even though the object was clearly moving — don't confuse 'zero displacement' with 'no motion occurred'.

sections.heading: 2.3 Average Velocity and Average Speed
sections.body:
Average velocity is displacement divided by the time interval over which it occurs; it is a vector and can be positive, negative or zero. Average speed is total path length divided by total time; it is a scalar and is always positive (or zero only if the body never moved).

Average speed is greater than or equal to the magnitude of average velocity, with equality only when the motion is one-directional (no reversal, no idle stop that isn't counted in the path). For a round trip, average velocity is zero but average speed is not, because the denominator (time) is the same but the numerator changes from displacement to path length.

Worked example: a car covers 100 km in 2 hours going out and 100 km in 3 hours coming back along the same road. Average speed = total distance / total time = 200/5 = 40 km/h. Average velocity = total displacement / total time = 0/5 = 0, since the car ends where it started.
sections.tip: If a question mixes two different speeds over two equal distances (not equal times), do NOT average the two speeds directly — use total distance / total time; this is the classic trap in 'average speed of a two-leg journey' problems.

sections.heading: 2.4 Instantaneous Velocity and Speed
sections.body:
Instantaneous velocity is the velocity of an object at one particular instant of time — the limit of average velocity as the time interval Δt shrinks to zero. Mathematically it is the derivative of position with respect to time: v = dx/dt. Geometrically, on a position–time graph, the instantaneous velocity at any point is the slope of the tangent to the curve at that point.

Instantaneous speed is simply the magnitude of the instantaneous velocity, |v|. Unlike average speed and average velocity, instantaneous speed and instantaneous velocity always have the same magnitude at every instant — there is no averaging over a path to create a difference between them.

Reading a position–time (x–t) graph is a core exam skill: a straight-line x–t graph means constant velocity (uniform motion); a curved x–t graph means the velocity is changing (non-uniform, accelerated motion); a horizontal line means the object is at rest; and a steeper slope always means a larger speed, regardless of the sign of the slope.

where: slope of the tangent to the x–t graph at that instant

sections.tip: On an x–t graph, a downward-sloping tangent means negative velocity (motion in the negative direction), not 'slowing down' — don't confuse the sign of slope with speeding up or slowing down; that needs the a–t or v–t graph.

sections.heading: 2.5 Acceleration
sections.body:
Average acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken: aavg = Δv/Δt. Instantaneous acceleration is the limit of this ratio as Δt → 0, i.e. a = dv/dt, the slope of the tangent to the velocity–time (v–t) graph at that instant. Since v = dx/dt, acceleration is also the second derivative of position: a = d²x/dt².

Acceleration is a vector; its sign shows direction, not simply 'speeding up' or 'slowing down'. An object speeds up when velocity and acceleration have the same sign, and slows down (decelerates) when they have opposite signs — regardless of whether acceleration itself is called 'positive' or 'negative' in the chosen convention. A body can have nonzero acceleration even at the instant its velocity is zero: at the highest point of a ball thrown straight up, v = 0 but a = −g (downward) throughout, because gravity never switches off.

On a v–t graph: the slope gives acceleration, and the area under the curve (between the curve and the time axis) gives the displacement over that interval. This area rule works even when acceleration is changing, because it comes directly from a = dv/dt and v = dx/dt.

where: instantaneous acceleration (m s<sup>−2</sup>), slope of the v–t graph

sections.tip: 'Retardation' or 'deceleration' just means acceleration opposite to velocity — always substitute it into the kinematic equations as a negative value of a (or u, depending on your sign convention), never as a separate rule.

sections.heading: 2.6 Position–Time and Velocity–Time Graphs
sections.body:
Graph questions are asked almost every year because they test understanding, not memorised formulas. Keep these rules fixed in mind:

  • On an x–t graph: slope = velocity. A straight line = uniform velocity; increasing slope with time = increasing velocity (accelerated motion); a horizontal segment = object at rest; a line crossing the time-axis means the object passes through the origin, not that it stops.
  • On a v–t graph: slope = acceleration; area between the curve and the time-axis = displacement. A straight horizontal line = zero acceleration (uniform velocity); a straight line with constant nonzero slope = uniform acceleration; area below the time axis counts as negative displacement.
  • On an a–t graph: area under the curve = change in velocity, Δv.

A v–t graph cannot be discontinuous with a sudden vertical jump in real motion (that would need infinite acceleration), and it cannot show two different velocities at the same instant of time — both are common 'which graph is not possible' MCQ traps. Similarly an x–t graph can never fold back on itself (be double-valued in x for one value of t), since an object cannot be at two positions at once.
sections.tip: When asked 'which of these graphs cannot represent the motion of a particle', check first for verticality (infinite speed/acceleration) and second for the graph doubling back on the time axis.

sections.heading: 2.7 Kinematic Equations for Uniformly Accelerated Motion
sections.body:
When acceleration a is constant, three equations connect initial velocity u, final velocity v, time t, acceleration a and displacement s. These can be derived either graphically (from the area and slope of a straight-line v–t graph) or by calculus (integrating a = dv/dt and v = dx/dt).

Calculus derivation of v = u + at: a = dv/dt is constant, so ∫uv dv = ∫0t a dt, giving v − u = at, i.e. v = u + at.

Calculus derivation of s = ut + ½at²: v = dx/dt = u + at, so ∫0s dx = ∫0t (u + at) dt, giving s = ut + ½at².

Calculus derivation of v² = u² + 2as: a = v(dv/dx) (using the chain rule, since a = dv/dt = (dv/dx)(dx/dt) = v dv/dx). So a dx = v dv, and integrating both sides, a∫0s dx = ∫uv v dv gives as = (v² − u²)/2, i.e. v² = u² + 2as.

A fourth useful (non-NCERT-numbered but frequently used) relation gives the distance covered in the nth second: sn = u + a(n − ½), obtained by subtracting the displacement up to (n−1) seconds from the displacement up to n seconds. These equations hold only when acceleration is uniform (constant in both magnitude and direction); for non-uniform acceleration you must go back to calculus or graphs.

where: connects velocity and displacement without time

sections.tip: The examiner rewards the derivation steps (the integration limits, or the area/slope construction on a v–t graph), not just the final boxed formula — write every step when a 'derive' question is asked.

sections.heading: 2.8 Motion Under Gravity: Free Fall as a Special Case
sections.body:
Free fall (dropping) and vertical throw (projected upward) are the most common application of the kinematic equations in Class 11 exams, because gravity provides a constant, known acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m s−2 directed downward (many textbooks and exam solutions round this to 10 m s−2 for simpler arithmetic; state the value you use).

Taking upward as positive: for a ball thrown up with initial speed u, acceleration is a = −g throughout the flight (even at the highest point, where v = 0 momentarily but a = −g never becomes zero). Time to reach maximum height, tup = u/g. Maximum height, hmax = u²/2g. If the ball returns to the point of projection, total time of flight T = 2u/g, and by symmetry the time to go up equals the time to come down, and the speed of return equals the launch speed u (ignoring air resistance).

Worked example: a ball is thrown vertically upward with u = 20 m s−1 (take g = 10 m s−2). Time to reach the top = u/g = 20/10 = 2 s. Maximum height = u²/2g = 400/20 = 20 m. Total time of flight = 2u/g = 4 s. Checking with s = ut + ½at² at t = 2 s: s = 20(2) − ½(10)(4) = 40 − 20 = 20 m — matches.

where: acceleration due to gravity, 9.8 m s<sup>−2</sup> (often taken as 10 m s<sup>−2</sup>)
total time of flight, up and back to the same level (s)

sections.tip: Always fix a sign convention first (say, up = positive) and stay with it for the whole problem — mixing signs mid-calculation is the single most common numerical error in free-fall questions.

sections.heading: 2.9 Relative Velocity
sections.body:
The relative velocity of object A with respect to object B is the velocity A appears to have as seen by an observer moving with B: vAB = vA − vB. In one dimension this is a straightforward subtraction with sign, but the sign convention must be applied carefully.

If two objects move in the same direction along a line with speeds vA and vB (vA > vB), the relative velocity of A with respect to B is vA − vB, and this is also the rate at which A gains on B — useful for 'time to overtake' problems. If they move in opposite directions, taking one direction as positive, the relative velocity is vA − (−vB) = vA + vB, i.e. the speeds add — this is why two vehicles approaching each other close the gap much faster than either one's own speed.

Worked example: two trains, each 100 m long, move on parallel tracks at 54 km/h and 36 km/h. (a) In the same direction: relative velocity = 54 − 36 = 18 km/h = 5 m/s; time to cross each other = (100+100)/5 = 40 s. (b) In opposite directions: relative velocity = 54 + 36 = 90 km/h = 25 m/s; time to cross = 200/25 = 8 s.

where: velocity of A relative to B (m s<sup>−1</sup>)
velocities of A and B in the ground frame, with sign (m s<sup>−1</sup>)

sections.tip: For 'two bodies moving towards each other' problems, add the speeds; for 'one chasing another in the same direction' problems, subtract them — read the direction words in the question very carefully before choosing which one to do.

key_terms.definition: An object whose size is negligible compared to the distance it moves, so its motion can be described by tracking a single point.
A coordinate system with a fixed origin and axes, with respect to which the position of an object is measured; motion is always described relative to a chosen frame.
The total length of the actual path travelled by an object; a scalar that never decreases.
The change in position of an object, Δx = x<sub>2</sub> − x<sub>1</sub>; a vector equal to the straight-line separation between initial and final positions.
Motion in which an object covers equal displacements in equal intervals of time; velocity is constant and the x–t graph is a straight line.
Motion in which velocity changes with time; the x–t graph is a curve and acceleration is nonzero.
Total displacement divided by the total time taken; a vector that can be zero even when the object moved.
Total path length divided by the total time taken; a scalar, always ≥ the magnitude of average velocity.
The velocity of an object at a particular instant, v = dx/dt, given by the slope of the tangent to the x–t graph at that point.
The rate of change of velocity at a particular instant, a = dv/dt, given by the slope of the tangent to the v–t graph at that point.
Motion in which acceleration is constant in both magnitude and direction, so the three kinematic equations (v = u+at, s = ut+½at², v² = u²+2as) apply.
Acceleration directed opposite to the velocity, causing the speed to decrease; used in equations as a negative value of a.
Motion of a body under gravity alone, with constant downward acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m s<sup>−2</sup>, ignoring air resistance.
The velocity of one object as measured by an observer moving with another object; v<sub>AB</sub> = v<sub>A</sub> − v<sub>B</sub>.
The total distance a vehicle travels from the moment the driver decides to stop (including the reaction-time distance) until it comes to rest.

diagrams.title: Position–time (x–t) graphs for different types of motion
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw four small x–t graphs side by side on the same x and t axes: (1) a horizontal straight line labelled 'at rest', (2) a straight line with positive slope labelled 'uniform velocity', (3) an upward-curving line (slope increasing with time) labelled 'uniformly accelerated, starting from rest', (4) a straight line with negative slope labelled 'uniform velocity in the negative direction'. Mark the slope at one point on graph 3 with a tangent line and label it 'instantaneous velocity = slope of tangent'.

diagrams.title: Velocity–time (v–t) graph for uniformly accelerated motion, with the area used to derive s = ut + ½at²
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a straight line starting at (0, u) on the v-axis and rising to (t, v) at time t, where v = u + at. Shade the trapezium area under the line between t = 0 and t. Split the trapezium into a rectangle of height u and width t (area = ut) sitting below a triangle of base t and height (v − u) = at (area = ½at²). Label the total shaded area as displacement s = ut + ½at², matching the algebraic derivation.

diagrams.title: Ball thrown vertically upward — velocity and acceleration at three points
diagrams.how_to_draw: Draw a vertical line showing the path of the ball with three marked points: the launch point (velocity u, upward arrow), the highest point (velocity = 0, but still draw a downward arrow labelled 'a = −g, never zero'), and the point of return (velocity u, downward arrow, same magnitude as launch by symmetry). Add a small v–t graph alongside it: a straight line starting at +u, crossing zero at t = u/g, and reaching −u at t = 2u/g, with constant negative slope −g throughout.

ncert_questions.q: In which of the following examples of motion, can the body be considered approximately a point object: (a) a railway carriage moving without jerks between two stations, (b) a monkey sitting on top of a man cycling smoothly on a circular track, (c) a spinning cricket ball that turns sharply on hitting the ground, (d) a tumbling beaker that has slipped off the edge of a table?
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Yes — the carriage travels a distance (the length of the track) much larger than its own size, so it can be treated as a point object.

(b) Yes — the monkey and cyclist together travel a distance around the track much larger than their size.

(c) No — the ball's own spin and the sharp turn it takes on hitting the ground depend on its size and orientation, which cannot be ignored.

(d) No — the beaker tumbles over a distance comparable to its own size, so its shape and orientation matter and it cannot be treated as a point.

ncert_questions.q: The position-time (x–t) graphs for two children A and B returning from their school O to their homes P and Q respectively are shown. Choose the correct entries in the brackets below: (a) A/B lives closer to the school than B/A. (b) A/B starts from the school earlier than B/A. (c) A/B walks faster than B/A. (d) A and B reach home at the (same/different) time. (e) A/B overtakes B/A on the road (once/twice).
ncert_questions.a:
(a) A lives closer to the school than B (A's line reaches a smaller final x value / P is nearer O than Q).

(b) A starts from the school earlier than B.

(c) B walks faster than A (B's x–t line has a steeper slope).

(d) A and B reach home at different times.

(e) B overtakes A on the road once (B starts later but, being faster, crosses A's path once before reaching home).

ncert_questions.q: A woman starts from her home at 9:00 am, walks with a speed of 5 km/h on a straight road up to her office 2.5 km away, stays at the office until 5:00 pm, and returns home by an auto with a speed of 25 km/h. Choose suitable scales and plot the x–t graph of her motion.
ncert_questions.a: Time to walk to office = distance/speed = 2.5/5 = 0.5 h = 30 min, so she reaches office at 9:30 am. The graph rises from x = 0 at t = 9:00 am to x = 2.5 km at t = 9:30 am, a straight line of positive slope 5 km/h. It then stays flat at x = 2.5 km from 9:30 am to 5:00 pm (she is stationary at office). Time for the return auto ride = 2.5/25 = 0.1 h = 6 min, so she is home by 5:06 pm; the graph falls steeply back to x = 0 between 5:00 pm and 5:06 pm, a straight line of slope −25 km/h (much steeper than the outward walk since the auto is faster).

ncert_questions.q: A drunkard walking in a narrow lane takes 5 steps forward and 3 steps backward, and so on, each step 1 m long and taking 1 s. Effectively he moves 8 m in 9 s (why?). Determine how long the drunkard takes to fall in a pit 13 m away from the start.
ncert_questions.a:
In every block of 8 s (5 forward + 3 backward steps), his net displacement is 5 − 3 = 2 m, so effectively he moves 2 m every 8 s.

After 4 such blocks (32 s), his net displacement = 4 × 2 = 8 m. In the next cycle he takes 5 more forward steps (5 s), reaching 8 + 5 = 13 m at the pit — so he falls into the pit exactly when his forward steps carry him there, without needing to step back. Time taken = 32 + 5 = 37 s.

ncert_questions.q: A car moving along a straight highway with a speed of 126 km/h is brought to a stop within a distance of 200 m. What is the retardation of the car (assumed uniform), and how long does it take for the car to stop?

A player throws a ball upwards with an initial speed of 29.4 m/s. (a) What is the direction of acceleration during the upward motion of the ball? (b) What are the velocity and acceleration of the ball at the highest point of its motion? (c) Choose the x = 0 m and t = 0 s to be the location and time of the ball at its highest point, vertically downward direction to be the positive direction of x-axis, and give the signs of position, velocity and acceleration of the ball during its downward motion. (d) To what height does the ball rise and after how long does the ball return to the player's hands? (Take g = 9.8 m/s<sup>2</sup> and neglect air resistance.)
ncert_questions.a:
(a) The acceleration is directed vertically downward (towards the ground) throughout the flight, since it is due to gravity alone; it does not reverse direction just because the ball is going up.

(b) At the highest point, velocity = 0, but acceleration = 9.8 m/s2 downward (unchanged) — velocity being zero does not mean acceleration is zero.

(c) With downward taken as positive and the highest point as origin: as the ball falls, position x is positive and increasing, velocity is positive and increasing, and acceleration is positive (= +g) throughout.

(d) Maximum height h = u2/2g = (29.4)2/(2 × 9.8) = 864.36/19.6 = 44.1 m. Total time of flight T = 2u/g = 2(29.4)/9.8 = 6.0 s.

ncert_questions.q: Explain clearly, with examples, the distinction between (a) magnitude of displacement (sometimes called distance) over an interval of time, and the total length of path covered by a particle over the same interval; (b) magnitude of average velocity over an interval of time, and the average speed over the same interval. Show in both (a) and (b) that the second quantity is either greater than or equal to the first. When is the equality sign true? (For simplicity, consider one-dimensional motion only.)
ncert_questions.a:
(a) Magnitude of displacement is the straight-line distance between the start and end position; path length is the total distance actually walked. Example: a person walks 5 m east then 3 m west — path length = 8 m, but magnitude of displacement = 2 m. Path length ≥ |displacement| always, because any deviation or reversal in the path only adds to the length walked without adding proportionally to the net separation.

(b) Average speed = path length/time, average velocity magnitude = |displacement|/time. Since path length ≥ |displacement| for the same time interval, average speed ≥ |average velocity|.

Equality holds in both cases only when the motion is strictly one-directional (the particle never reverses direction), so that path length exactly equals the magnitude of displacement.

ncert_questions.q: A car moves from X to Y with a uniform speed v<sub>u</sub> and returns to X with a uniform speed v<sub>d</sub>. What is the average speed for this round trip?
ncert_questions.a:
Let the one-way distance be d. Time for X→Y = d/vu; time for Y→X = d/vd. Total distance = 2d; total time = d/vu + d/vd = d(vu+vd)/(vuvd).

Average speed = total distance/total time = 2d ÷ [d(vu+vd)/(vuvd)] = 2vuvd/(vu+vd). This is the harmonic mean of the two speeds, not their simple average — a common exam trap.

ncert_questions.q: Two trains A and B of length 400 m each are moving on two parallel tracks with a uniform speed of 72 km/h in the same direction, with A ahead of B. The driver of B decides to overtake A and accelerates by 1 m/s<sup>2</sup>. If after 50 s, the guard of B just brushes past the driver of A, what was the original distance between them?
ncert_questions.a:
Both trains start with the same speed 72 km/h = 20 m/s, so B's initial velocity relative to A is 0. Since A moves at constant velocity, B's acceleration relative to A equals B's own acceleration, a = 1 m/s2.

Relative displacement of B's front with respect to A's front in t = 50 s: s = 0(50) + ½(1)(50)2 = 1250 m.

This 1250 m is the distance B's front gains on A's front. For B's guard (at the rear of B, 400 m behind B's front) to just reach A's driver (at the front of A), B's front must have advanced 1250 m relative to A's front, which equals: (original gap between B's front and A's rear) + (length of A, 400 m, since B's front must pass all of A) − (length of B, 400 m, since it is the rear of B, not the front, that needs to reach A's front). These two 400 m lengths cancel, so the original gap between the two trains = 1250 m − 400 m = 850 m (subtracting train A's length, following the standard NCERT solution method).

ncert_questions.q: On a two-lane road, car A is travelling with a speed of 36 km/h. Two cars B and C approach car A in opposite directions with a speed of 54 km/h each. At a certain instant, when the distance AB is equal to AC, both being 1 km, B decides to overtake A before C does. What minimum acceleration of car B is required to avoid an accident?
ncert_questions.a:
Convert to m/s: vA = 36 km/h = 10 m/s, vB = vC = 54 km/h = 15 m/s.

Relative velocity of B with respect to A (both initially moving towards each other, B behind A in the same lane direction as A but overtaking, C approaching A from the front) = 15 − 10 = 5 m/s... Following the standard NCERT solution: relative velocity of C with respect to A (approaching, opposite direction) = 15 + 10 = 25 m/s. Time for C to cover the 1 km gap to A: t = 1000/25 = 40 s. This is the time B has to complete the overtake.

Relative velocity of B with respect to A (B behind A, same direction) = 15 − 10 = 5 m/s. In 40 s at this relative velocity, B would only close 5 × 40 = 200 m of the 1000 m gap, so B needs additional relative acceleration a to cover the full 1000 m: 1000 = 5(40) + ½a(40)2 ⟹ 1000 − 200 = 800a ⟹ a = 800/800 = 1 m/s2.

pyq.q: A body is thrown vertically upward. Which of the following remains constant during its flight (ignoring air resistance)?
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Acceleration due to gravity stays at g downward throughout the flight; velocity and speed change continuously and displacement is not constant, it grows and then reverses.

pyq.q: The area under a velocity–time graph, between the curve and the time axis, represents:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Since v = dx/dt, integrating v over time (the area under the v–t curve) gives the displacement over that interval.

pyq.q: A particle moves in a straight line and returns to its starting point after 20 s, having covered a total path length of 60 m. Its average velocity for this interval is:
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Average velocity = displacement/time. Since the particle returns to its starting point, displacement = 0, so average velocity = 0, regardless of the path length covered.

pyq.q: Two cars A and B move in the same direction on a straight road at 20 m/s and 15 m/s respectively. The velocity of A relative to B is:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: For motion in the same direction, relative velocity = v_A − v_B = 20 − 15 = 5 m/s.

pyq.q: On a position–time graph, a straight horizontal line parallel to the time axis represents:
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: A horizontal line means position x does not change with time, so the object is stationary; its slope (velocity) is zero throughout.

pyq.q: A ball is dropped from a height and falls freely under gravity. Its speed–time graph is:
options: A straight line through the origin with positive slope
A straight line not passing through the origin, with zero slope
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: For free fall from rest, v = gt, which is a straight line through the origin with constant slope g.

pyq.q: The displacement of a particle is given by x = 3t<sup>2</sup> + 2t + 5 (SI units). Its acceleration is:
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: v = dx/dt = 6t + 2; a = dv/dt = 6 m/s<sup>2</sup>, a constant, independent of t.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The speed of a particle can never be negative. Reason (R): Speed is the magnitude of velocity, and the magnitude of a vector quantity is always non-negative.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Speed = |velocity|, and magnitude by definition is always ≥ 0, which directly and correctly explains why speed is never negative.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): A particle can have zero velocity but nonzero acceleration at the same instant. Reason (R): At the highest point of a vertically thrown ball, velocity is zero but the acceleration due to gravity continues to act.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: This is a standard true case, correctly explained: gravity does not switch off when v = 0; a = −g remains throughout the flight, giving exactly the example claimed in R.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Average speed of a body can never be less than the magnitude of its average velocity. Reason (R): Path length covered by a body is always greater than or equal to the magnitude of its displacement.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Average speed = path length/time and |average velocity| = |displacement|/time, over the same time interval; since path length ≥ |displacement| (R), average speed ≥ |average velocity| (A), and R correctly explains A.

pyq.q: Can a body have zero velocity and still be accelerating? Give one example.
pyq.answer: Yes. At the highest point of a ball thrown vertically upward, its velocity is momentarily zero, but the acceleration due to gravity (g, directed downward) continues to act on it throughout, since gravity does not stop acting just because the velocity is zero at that instant.

pyq.q: A particle moves along the x-axis such that its position is x = 2t<sup>3</sup> − 3t<sup>2</sup> + 4 (SI units). Find its velocity and acceleration at t = 2 s.
State two differences between distance and displacement.
pyq.answer:
(1) Distance (path length) is a scalar quantity with only magnitude; displacement is a vector quantity with magnitude and direction.
(2) Distance can never decrease and is always positive for a moving body; displacement can be positive, negative or zero, and its magnitude can be less than, but never more than, the distance travelled.

pyq.q: What does the slope of a velocity–time graph represent? What does the area under it represent?
pyq.answer: The slope of a v–t graph at any point gives the instantaneous acceleration at that instant (a = dv/dt). The area enclosed between the v–t curve and the time axis, over a given time interval, gives the displacement of the object during that interval.

pyq.q: A car travels the first half of a distance between two places at a speed of 30 km/h and the second half at a speed of 50 km/h. Find the average speed of the car for the whole journey.
pyq.answer: Average speed for equal distances at two different speeds is the harmonic mean: v<sub>avg</sub> = 2v<sub>1</sub>v<sub>2</sub>/(v<sub>1</sub>+v<sub>2</sub>) = 2(30)(50)/(30+50) = 3000/80 = 37.5 km/h.

pyq.q: Derive the equation s = ut + ½at<sup>2</sup> for uniformly accelerated motion using the velocity–time graph.
pyq.answer:
Consider a v–t graph where velocity increases uniformly from u at t = 0 to v at time t, a straight line. The displacement s equals the area under this line, which is a trapezium.
Split the trapezium into a rectangle of height u and base t (area = ut) and a triangle sitting above it with base t and height (v − u) (area = ½ t(v − u)).
Since a = (v − u)/t, we have (v − u) = at, so the triangle's area = ½at2.
Total area (= displacement) s = ut + ½at2.

pyq.q: A car starts from rest and accelerates uniformly at 2 m/s<sup>2</sup> for 10 s. It then continues at the constant velocity reached for 20 s, and finally decelerates uniformly to rest in 5 s. Find (a) the maximum velocity reached, (b) the total distance travelled.
pyq.answer:
(a) v = u + at = 0 + 2(10) = 20 m/s.
(b) Stage 1 (0–10 s, accelerating): s1 = ut + ½at2 = 0 + ½(2)(100) = 100 m.
Stage 2 (10–30 s, constant 20 m/s): s2 = 20 × 20 = 400 m.
Stage 3 (last 5 s, decelerating from 20 m/s to 0): s3 = (u+v)/2 × t = (20+0)/2 × 5 = 50 m.
Total distance = 100 + 400 + 50 = 550 m.

pyq.q: A stone is dropped from the top of a tower 45 m high, and at the same time another stone is thrown upward from the ground with a velocity of 20 m/s along the same vertical line. Find when and where the two stones meet. (Take g = 10 m/s<sup>2</sup>.)
pyq.answer:
Let the height of the tower be H = 45 m, and let x be the distance the dropped stone falls before meeting.
Dropped stone (from top, taking downward positive): x = ½gt2 = 5t2.
Thrown-up stone (from ground, taking upward positive): height risen y = 20t − ½gt2 = 20t − 5t2.
They meet when the distance fallen plus the height risen equals the tower height: x + y = 45 ⟹ 5t2 + 20t − 5t2 = 45 ⟹ 20t = 45 ⟹ t = 2.25 s.
Distance fallen by dropped stone: x = 5(2.25)2 = 5(5.0625) = 25.3 m, so they meet 25.3 m below the top of the tower (i.e. 45 − 25.3 = 19.7 m above the ground).

pyq.q: A body travels a distance of 20 m in the 7th second and 24 m in the 9th second. Assuming uniform acceleration, find the initial velocity and the acceleration of the body.
pyq.answer:
Using sn = u + a(n − ½):
s7 = u + a(6.5) = 20
s9 = u + a(8.5) = 24
Subtracting: a(8.5 − 6.5) = 24 − 20 ⟹ 2a = 4 ⟹ a = 2 m/s2.
Substituting back: u + 2(6.5) = 20 ⟹ u + 13 = 20 ⟹ u = 7 m/s.

pyq.q: Derive the three equations of motion (v = u + at, s = ut + ½at<sup>2</sup>, v<sup>2</sup> = u<sup>2</sup> + 2as) for uniformly accelerated motion using calculus. Then use them to solve: a bullet fired into a fixed target loses half its velocity after penetrating 3 cm. Find how much further it will penetrate before coming to rest, assuming it faces uniform retardation.
pyq.answer:
Derivations:
Since a = dv/dt is constant, ∫uvdv = ∫0ta·dt ⟹ v − u = at ⟹ v = u + at.
Since v = dx/dt = u + at, ∫0sdx = ∫0t(u+at)dt ⟹ s = ut + ½at2.
Since a = v(dv/dx) (chain rule), a·dx = v·dv, so a∫0sdx = ∫uvv·dv ⟹ as = (v2−u2)/2 ⟹ v2 = u2 + 2as.
Application: Let initial speed = u, after 3 cm speed = u/2. Using v2 = u2 + 2as: (u/2)2 = u2 + 2a(3) ⟹ u2/4 − u2 = 6a ⟹ −3u2/4 = 6a ⟹ a = −u2/8 (retardation).
Now find further penetration distance d, from speed u/2 to 0: 0 = (u/2)2 + 2a·d ⟹ 0 = u2/4 + 2(−u2/8)d ⟹ u2/4 = (u2/4)d ⟹ d = 1 cm.

pyq.q: State what is meant by relative velocity in one dimension, and derive the expression for the relative velocity of one object with respect to another. Then solve: a jet airplane travelling at 500 km/h ejects its products of combustion at a speed of 1500 km/h relative to the jet plane. Find the speed of the ejected gases relative to the ground observer.
pyq.answer:
Concept: If two objects A and B move along the same straight line with velocities vA and vB (measured from a common ground frame, with sign), the velocity of A as seen by an observer moving with B is the relative velocity vAB = vA − vB. This follows because, in the frame moving with B, B's own velocity appears to be zero, so every other velocity must be reduced by vB.
Application: Take the direction of the jet's motion as positive. Jet's velocity vjet = +500 km/h. The exhaust gas moves backward relative to the jet at 1500 km/h, so its velocity relative to the jet, vgas,jet = −1500 km/h.
Velocity of gas relative to ground: vgas = vgas,jet + vjet = −1500 + 500 = −1000 km/h.
So the ejected gas moves at 1000 km/h in the direction opposite to the jet's motion, as seen from the ground.

pyq.q: A driver sees a red traffic light and applies brakes 0.5 s after seeing it (reaction time). If the car was moving at 54 km/h and decelerates uniformly at 6 m/s<sup>2</sup> once the brakes are applied, find (a) the distance travelled during the reaction time, (b) the braking distance after the brakes are applied, (c) the total stopping distance, and explain how reaction time affects stopping distance in general.
pyq.answer:
u = 54 km/h = 15 m/s.
(a) During reaction time, the car moves at constant speed (brakes not yet applied): distance = u × tr = 15 × 0.5 = 7.5 m.
(b) After braking, using v2 = u2 + 2as with v = 0, u = 15 m/s, a = −6 m/s2: 0 = (15)2 − 2(6)s ⟹ s = 225/12 = 18.75 m.
(c) Total stopping distance = 7.5 + 18.75 = 26.25 m.
In general, the reaction-time distance grows linearly with speed (u·tr), while the braking distance grows with the square of speed (u2/2a); this is why stopping distance increases sharply, not just proportionally, as speed goes up, which is the physics reason speed limits matter more than they seem to at first glance.

pyq.q:
A car starts from rest at a traffic signal and accelerates uniformly at 3 m/s2 for 8 seconds. It then moves at the constant velocity it has reached for the next 12 seconds, and finally the driver applies brakes, bringing the car to rest with uniform retardation in 4 seconds.
(i) What is the velocity of the car at the end of the acceleration phase?
(ii) What is the distance covered during the acceleration phase?
(iii) What is the distance covered during the constant-velocity phase?
(iv) What is the retardation during braking, and the total distance covered by the car in its entire journey?
pyq.answer:
(i) v = u + at = 0 + 3(8) = 24 m/s.
(ii) s1 = ut + ½at2 = 0 + ½(3)(64) = 96 m.
(iii) s2 = velocity × time = 24 × 12 = 288 m.
(iv) Retardation: using v = u + at with v = 0, u = 24 m/s, t = 4 s: 0 = 24 + a(4) ⟹ a = −6 m/s2, so retardation = 6 m/s2. Distance in braking phase, s3 = (u+v)/2 × t = (24+0)/2 × 4 = 48 m. Total distance = 96 + 288 + 48 = 432 m.

pyq.q:
Two friends, Rohan and Simran, start from the same point on a straight road at the same instant. Rohan walks at a constant speed of 5 km/h. Simran starts 0.4 hours (24 minutes) later on a bicycle at a constant speed of 15 km/h, along the same road in the same direction.
(i) How far has Rohan walked by the time Simran starts?
(ii) What is the velocity of Simran relative to Rohan once Simran starts moving?
(iii) How long after Simran starts does she catch up with Rohan?
(iv) At what distance from the starting point does Simran catch up with Rohan?
pyq.answer:
(i) Distance = speed × time = 5 × 0.4 = 2 km.
(ii) Both move in the same direction, so relative velocity of Simran with respect to Rohan = 15 − 5 = 10 km/h.
(iii) Simran must close the 2 km gap at a relative speed of 10 km/h: time = distance/relative velocity = 2/10 = 0.2 h = 12 minutes.
(iv) Distance covered by Simran in that time = 15 × 0.2 = 3 km from the starting point (check: Rohan's total time is 0.4 + 0.2 = 0.6 h, distance = 5 × 0.6 = 3 km — matches).

practice_mcq.q: The displacement of a particle moving in a straight line is given by x = 5 + 3t − 2t<sup>2</sup> (SI units). What is its initial velocity?
practice_mcq.explanation: v = dx/dt = 3 − 4t. At t = 0, v = 3 m/s.

practice_mcq.q: A particle covers half of its total distance with speed v<sub>1</sub> and the rest with speed v<sub>2</sub>. Its average speed during the whole journey is:
practice_mcq.explanation: For equal distances at two speeds, average speed is the harmonic mean, 2v1v2/(v1+v2), not the arithmetic mean.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following can never be negative for a moving particle?
practice_mcq.explanation: Speed is the magnitude of velocity and magnitudes are never negative; displacement, velocity and acceleration can all be negative depending on the sign convention.

practice_mcq.q: A body starts from rest and moves with uniform acceleration. The ratio of distances covered in the first, second and third seconds is:
practice_mcq.explanation: Distance in nth second for u=0 is s_n = a(n − ½), so for n=1,2,3 the ratios are 0.5a : 1.5a : 2.5a = 1 : 3 : 5.

practice_mcq.q: A stone is dropped from a height h and reaches the ground in time T. From what height should it be dropped to reach the ground in time 2T (same g)?
practice_mcq.explanation: h = ½gt<sup>2</sup>, so h ∝ t<sup>2</sup>. Doubling t means height must become 4 times, so height = 4h.

practice_mcq.q: On a v–t graph, if the line has a negative slope but lies entirely above the time axis, the object is:
options: Speeding up in the positive direction
Moving in the positive direction but decelerating
practice_mcq.explanation: v remains positive (above the axis) so the object still moves in the positive direction, but negative slope means acceleration is negative — velocity is decreasing, i.e. decelerating.

practice_mcq.q: Two objects A and B move towards each other on a straight line with speeds 8 m/s and 12 m/s respectively. Their relative velocity of approach is:
practice_mcq.explanation: For objects moving towards each other (opposite directions), relative velocity of approach = sum of speeds = 8 + 12 = 20 m/s.

practice_mcq.q: A body moving with uniform acceleration has velocities of 20 m/s and 30 m/s when it passes two points 135 m apart. What is its acceleration?
The area under an acceleration–time (a–t) graph gives:
practice_mcq.explanation: Since a = dv/dt, integrating a over time gives Δv, the change in velocity — not displacement.

practice_mcq.q: A ball is thrown vertically upward and returns to the thrower's hand after 6 s. Taking g = 10 m/s<sup>2</sup>, its initial speed was:
A particle's position–time graph is a straight line inclined to the time axis but not passing through the origin. This shows the particle:
options: Started from the origin with zero velocity
Started from a nonzero initial position and moved with uniform velocity
practice_mcq.explanation: A straight line means constant velocity (uniform motion); not passing through the origin only means the particle's starting position was not x = 0.

practice_mcq.q: A car moving at 20 m/s is stopped by applying brakes that produce a uniform retardation of 4 m/s<sup>2</sup>. The distance covered by the car before it stops is:
For a particle undergoing one-dimensional motion, which statement is always true?
options: Average speed equals magnitude of average velocity
Magnitude of average velocity can exceed average speed
Average speed is always ≥ magnitude of average velocity
Average speed is always less than magnitude of average velocity
practice_mcq.explanation: Path length ≥ |displacement| always, so dividing both by the same time interval gives average speed ≥ |average velocity|, with equality only for one-directional motion.

practice_mcq.q: A body covers 100 m in the 5th second and 130 m in the 7th second, moving with uniform acceleration. Its acceleration is:
Which of these v–t graphs is NOT physically possible for the motion of a real particle?
options: A straight line with constant positive slope
A vertical straight line (velocity changing instantly at one instant)
A curve that smoothly changes slope with time
practice_mcq.explanation: A vertical line on a v–t graph would mean velocity changes by a finite amount in zero time, i.e. infinite acceleration, which is not physically possible for a real body.

practice_mcq.q: A person walks 3 km east, then 4 km north. The magnitude of the person's total displacement is:
practice_mcq.explanation: Using the Pythagorean theorem for perpendicular displacements: √(3²+4²) = √25 = 5 km. (Path length is 7 km, but displacement magnitude is 5 km — this tests the distinction directly.)

common_mistakes: Treating distance and displacement as the same thing, especially in round-trip problems where displacement is zero but distance is not.
Averaging two speeds directly (arithmetic mean) for a journey covering equal distances at different speeds, instead of using total distance/total time (the harmonic mean).
Assuming acceleration must be zero when velocity is zero — missing the classic case of the highest point of a vertical throw, where v = 0 but a = −g.
Mixing sign conventions midway through a free-fall or braking problem (switching what 'positive' means partway through the calculation), which flips the sign of the final answer.
Reading the slope of an x–t graph as speed only, without noting that a negative slope means motion in the negative direction, not 'the object is slowing down'.
Forgetting that the kinematic equations (v=u+at, s=ut+½at², v²=u²+2as) apply only to uniform (constant) acceleration, and trying to use them directly when acceleration itself is changing.
In relative-velocity problems, subtracting speeds when the two bodies move in opposite directions (should add) or adding when they move in the same direction (should subtract).
Forgetting to convert km/h to m/s (÷3.6, or ×5/18) before substituting into the SI kinematic equations, which is one of the most common numerical slips.
strategy:
This chapter rewards understanding over memorising formulas, because most marks lost in the school final come from graph-reading and sign-convention slips, not from forgetting the equations. Start by making sure the distance-vs-displacement and average-speed-vs-average-velocity distinctions are automatic — several 1-mark and assertion-reason questions test nothing but this.

Learn the three kinematic equations well enough to derive them two ways: from a v–t graph (area and slope) and by calculus (integrating a = dv/dt and v = dx/dt). Boards and school finals that ask for a 'derivation' give marks for each correct step, so write the full working, not just the final boxed result.

Practice reading x–t, v–t and a–t graphs until you can instantly say what slope and area mean on each — this is the fastest-scoring skill in the chapter once it clicks. For numericals, always fix a sign convention (write it down) before substituting, convert every speed to consistent SI units first, and keep free-fall and relative-velocity problems as two separate mental templates so you don't mix their sign rules. Finally, work through the NCERT exercise and exemplar problems fully at least once — several of the case-based and long-answer questions in school finals are close variants of these.
revision_checklist: I can state the difference between distance and displacement with an example where they differ.
I can state the difference between average speed and average velocity, and know average speed ≥ |average velocity|.
I know average speed for a two-leg equal-distance journey is the harmonic mean, not the arithmetic mean, of the two speeds.
I can define instantaneous velocity as dx/dt and identify it as the slope of the tangent to an x–t graph.
I can define instantaneous acceleration as dv/dt and identify it as the slope of the tangent to a v–t graph.
I can explain why a body can have zero velocity but nonzero acceleration, with the vertical-throw example.
I can derive all three kinematic equations both graphically and by calculus, showing every step.
I can solve a free-fall (drop or vertical throw) problem for maximum height, time up, and total time of flight.
I know the kinematic equations apply only when acceleration is uniform.
I can read any x–t, v–t or a–t graph and state what the slope and the area under it represent.
I can identify which of a set of given v–t or x–t graphs is not physically possible, and explain why.
I can set up and solve a relative-velocity problem for bodies moving in the same and in opposite directions.
I can solve a stopping-distance problem that combines a reaction-time phase and a braking phase.
I always fix a sign convention and convert units to SI before starting a numerical.
I have solved every NCERT in-chapter and exercise question at least once without looking at the solution first.
